Noncovalent interactions (NCIs), such as hydrogen bond, halo-
gen bond, hydrophobic effect, π-stacking, etc., have been inte-
gral to biocatalysis, and their application to chemical catalysis
has been accelerated over the past two decades. Although the
underpinning of these relatively complex interactions is still
a challenging foray, advancement in density functional the-
ory and high-level calculations with wave-function-based quan-
tum mechanical approaches have led to reliable interpretations
of these weak interactions, with sufficient accuracy, to pro-
vide meaningful insights on their physical origins in molecular
binding and chemical transformations. Such an in-depth under-
standing of electronic structure and reactivity offers possibilities
for judicious engineering of these complex intra/intermolecular
interactions to achieve enzyme-like optimum efficacy. In this
study, we therefore focus on applications that demonstrate the
advantages of rational manipulation of noncovalent interactions
in molecular and supramolecular organocatalytic frameworks,
pertaining to chiral catalysis, electron-donor acceptor events in
photo-redox catalysis, or transformations within confined spaces
of self-assembled capsules and cages. We emphasize on how
quantum chemical data analysis provides reasonable indications
of catalyst performance. We also highlight the ongoing chal-
lenges in computing reaction outcomes and discuss remedial
approaches. We believe this overview would provide guiding
principles for the successful designing of organo-catalysts using
noncovalent weak interactions.

1.1. Hydrogen Bonding
Hydrogen bonding (HB) is by far the most versatile and explored
noncovalent interaction in molecular assemblage (Scheme 1). It
functionally “glues” and controls the structural features of the
building blocks of life, like water, DNA, protein, etc. It is primarily
a local electrostatic bonding interaction between a donor (D-
H) and an acceptor unit (A). The cumulative effect of different
attractive forces, such as charge transfer, induction, and dis-
persion forces, renders significant strength to H-bonds at short
distances, for e.g., during proton transport in condensed media
(Figure 1a).[6a] Perhaps, the Grotthuss mechanism proposed in
1806 is the most well-accepted explanation of the cooperativity
in H-bonds, which propels excess proton solvation and trans-
port in aqueous media.[6b] Although debatable, this mechanism
suggests that networks of cooperative hydrogen bonding lead
to the proton mobility, and the excess protonic charge shut-
tles through strings of water molecules, leaving no room for
free protons.[6c] However, recent developments, supported by
IR spectra, discuss isomerization between [(H2O)nH+] ions as
an outcome of hydrogen bond cleavage in the second solva-
tion sphere that triggers formation of a new hydrogen bond
at a low activation barrier (2.6 kcal/mol) and facilitates a peri-
odic series of isomerizations.[6d] Recent experimental work by
Hunter and coworkers demonstrates that, in non-aqueous sys-
tems such as phenol oligomers, hydrogen-bond cooperativity
is inherently dictated by pairwise local interactions between
adjacent neighbors.[6e] It has been found that cooperative hydro-
gen bonds between hydroxyl groups enhance the formation
of the first intermolecular H-bond with quinuclidine by up
to 14 kJ mol−1. Incidentally, H-bond cooperativity is controlled
by polarization and secondary electrostatic interactions. Hence,
in addition to a direct H-bond between quinuclidine (H-bond
acceptor) and phenol (H-bond donor), long-range electrostatic
effects beyond neighboring hydroxyl pairs stabilize the overall
complex.[6e]
1.2. Halogen Bonding
Recently, halogen bonding (XB) has garnered much attention
due to its promising functionalization in directing molecular
self-assembly phenomenon, molecular recognition devices, crys-
tal engineering and biological applications.[7] However, since
Colin’s discovery of the first halogen-bonded XB adduct, I2•••NH3,
the underlying physical nature of this crucial interaction is
still debated.[8a] Early discoveries of 1:1 dimers of Br2 and Cl2
with amines, and XB adducts such as F2•••NH3 and F2•••OH2
suggested that the strength of halogen bonds are described
by the polarizability of the XB donors in the following order
F < Cl < Br < I, where F being the least polarizable. Expect-
edly, F is involved as XB donor only when attached to very
strong electron-withdrawing groups.[8a,b] Later, independent pio-
neering discoveries by Mulliken on chemical bond (Nobel Prize
in chemistry in 1966), and Hassel on conformational studies
(Noble Prize in chemistry in 1969), constituted rationalization
of colored solution of I2 dissolved in organic solvents on the
basis of intermolecular donor–acceptor interactions.[8a] It was
propounded further by UV-vis spectroscopy that all such com-
plexes consisted of charge-transfer to the halogen.[8c] Latest
reports indicate that halogen bonding is primarily a net attrac-
tive electrostatic potential between a lower electron density
region (or the σ-hole) close to a halogen atom (halogen-bond
donor) and a nucleophilic region with large electron density
(halogen-bond acceptor), in a direction orthogonal to the nor-
mal covalent bond associated with the halogen atom, because of
the anisotropic distribution of its electron density (Figure 1b).[8d]
For example, the X-ray crystal structure of the adduct between 5-
iodouracil and 1,3-dimethyl-2(3H)-imidazoleselone reveals a I─Se
halogen bond (at a distance of 3.37 Å), due to the polariza-
tion of the C═Se bond in presence of the proximal iodine atom
(Figure 1b).[8d] Further, mapping of the electrostatic potential
around the adduct demonstrates existence of a σ-hole on the
iodine atom and a negative charge density on selenium, indi-
cating significant selenolate character, conducive for halogen
bonding (Figure 1b).[8d] This definition is elegantly rational-
ized by Politzer’s σ-hole concept, where halogen atoms behave
as electrophiles.[8e] Although, electrostatics play a key role in
halogen bonding, the close approach of two highly polariz-
able atoms—the halogen and the electron donor—often within
less than the sum of their van der Waals radii, means that
polarization and dispersion contributions are also significant.
Recently, Hobza and others proposed that electrostatic inter-
action is complemented by London dispersion during halogen
bonding. Furthermore, the authors report that heavier halogen

1.3. π-Stacking
Other relevant NCIs include π aromatic systems such as π–
π, XH–π, cation–π, anion–π
and lone-pair–π
interactions
(Scheme 1), which are ubiquitous in several biological and mate-
rial structures.[1c,9] For instance, the redox behavior of quinones
is quite complex and strongly affected by the chemical environ-
ment. While in buffered water, quinone undergoes reduction
to hydroquinone through a 2e−/2H+ process, in unbuffered
water it prefers to form the strongly hydrogen-bonded quinone
dianion, undergoing a 2e−reduction process (Figure 1c).[10a]
Incidentally, nature utilizes this unique property of quinone to
fine-tune the redox activity of complex I (NADH:ubiquinone
oxidoreductase, Figure 1c).[10b] Analysis of the binding modes of
ubiquinone (UQ) and menaquinone (MQ) to complex I shows
that hydrogen-bonded binding mode of UQ/MQ with His-38
and Tyr-87 is energetically less favorable (by ∼2 kcal/mol) over
the stacked Q conformation featuring dispersive interaction
of UQ/MQ with His-38, while remaining H-bonded to Tyr-87
(Figure 1c).[10b] Such conformational changes in the binding
modes of quinone leads to modulation of redox potentials by
>200 mV, attributed to optimum positioning of dispersive π−π
interactions, causing lowered shifts in redox potentials relative to
H-bond.[10b] A deeper understanding on π-stacking interactions
are based on the original Hunter–Sanders model which uti-
lizes charge-distribution to explain the strength and geometric
preferences in aromatic systems.[10c] The model considers each
aromatic ring centers as a local quadrupole due to the positively
charged nucleus and a pair of negative charges above and
below the molecular plane at a distance d. It attributed the pre-
ferred π–π stacking geometries, particularly the T-shaped and
parallel-displaced arrangements due to quadrupole–quadrupole
interactions
arising
from
aromatic
ring
polarization.[10c]

Subsequent work highlighted the importance of electrostatics in
modulating substituent effects in π-stacking interactions. Cor-
relations were drawn between electrostatic interactions of the
local dipoles emerging due to substituents and the electric field
of the other aromatic ring.[10d,e] Particularly, electron-accepting
substituents, such as ─CN and ─NO2 were found to enhance
π-stacking interactions by reducing the electronic repulsion
between the π-electron clouds; whereas electron donating
substituents were found to hinder such interactions.[10d] This

molecular quadrupole moments.[10f] However, the underlying
concept of strong stacking interactions arising between arenes
with complementary electronic disposition was questioned,
particularly in systems having electron-deficient arenes (for
instance naphthalene diimides).[10e] More recently, Wheeler’s
computational reinvestigation of the Hunter–Sanders model
demonstrated that the preference for parallel-displaced π-
stacking is better explained by the interplay between dispersion
forces and Pauli repulsion, which more accurately accounts for
the observed offset in geometry.[10g]
1.4. Hydrophobic Effect
Lately, hydrophobic interactions have been identified in ionic liq-
uids, their self-assembly into micelles or liquid crystals,[11] or in
MOF cavities having long alkyl chains anchored to their organic
linkers.[12] Systematically tuned hydrophobic forces inside the
MOF cavities create a unique spatial environment surround-
ing the active catalytic sites that is challenging to achieve in
typical organocatalysts.[12a] However, unlike other noncovalent
interactions, the hydrophobic effect is not a direct interaction
between two molecules, rather soft forces that depends on
the physiochemical properties of the solution, such as tempera-
ture, pressure, presence of additives, solvent dielectric constant,
etc. In hydrophobic solvation, the solute-water interfacial free
energy is higher than bulk water-water interaction, leading to
the formation of cage structure of H-bonded water around the
dissolved aggregated solutes. Thus, the entropic cost of order-
ing water molecules around nonpolar solutes, results in a large
thermodynamically unfavorable entropy change (−TS > 0) that
dominates the free energy penalty of hydrophobic solvation,
even though the associated enthalpy change (H) is minimal
or close to zero.[12b] The hydrophobic effect, therefore, not only
modulates the rate of a reaction, but also governs the final prod-
uct distribution and influences the overall selectivity.[12c] One
interesting example is the oxidation of benzylic compounds in
Cr3+- and Fe3+-containing terephthalate MOFs known as MIL-
101.[12c] MIL-101(Cr) reported 87% selectivity while MIL-101(Fe)
reported 71% selectivity for oxidation of indane to the corre-
sponding alcohol-ketone mixture (Figure 1d). This variation in
selectivity was primarily because of the higher hydrophobic
character inside the MIL-101(Cr) cavity, that preferentially adsorbs
new incoming indane from the bulk solution, allowing diffusion
of the indanol–indanone mixture out of the hydrophobic MOF
pore.

1.5. Computational Methods to Account NCIs
Over the years, density functional (DFT) calculations have
become extremely useful in understanding reaction mechanisms
and interpreting factors responsible for regio- and enantiose-
lectivities by identifying the crucial transition states.[13] Com-
putations of energies and reaction barriers and construction
of Gibbs free energy profiles provide quantitative understand-
ing on reaction acceleration by lowered activation energy on
employing a suitable catalyst, working at ambient to moderate
temperature and other external conditions (Figure 2a). Insights
gained from DFT calculations pave the path for rational design
of more selective and optimum catalytic systems.[13] Significant
progress has also been made to evaluate the key noncova-
lent interactions in organocatalytic reactions with the help of
DFT. Conventional DFT hybrid functionals such as B3LYP[14] strug-
gle to accurately capture NCIs, due to their inherent limitations
in describing long-range dispersion forces. This has led to a

2. Harnessing Noncovalent Interactions in
Asymmetric Organo-Catalysis
Identification of effective organo-catalysts that could steer direc-
tions toward desired selectivity is of paramount importance in
synthetic organic chemistry. Presently, most catalysts are dis-
covered through a trial-and-error method, commensurate with
extensive resource utilization, with little emphasis on process
sustainability. However, modifying existing catalysts with tar-
geted functionalities and judiciously customizing their structure
as per need, with the help of in silico tools, assists in pre-
dicting experimental outcomes. Thus, calculations have led to
qualitative understanding and quantitative screening of catalytic
models to be prepared and tested.
2.1. Asymmetric Anti-Mannich Product by
Pyrrolidine-Carboxylic Acid
One of the first examples of a computational design of an
organocatalyst prior to synthesis was conducted by the groups
of Houk and Barbas.[23] The authors reported that natural
amino acids such as (S)-proline delivered (2S,3S)-syn-amino alde-
hydes with high enantioselectivities on asymmetric Mannich
reaction between aldehydes and N-p-methoxyphenyl (PMP)
protected imines (Scheme 2, top), while non-asymmetric anti-
Mannich products were seldom found.[23] Houk et. al had
earlier reported the preference for a s-trans-enamine geome-

4. Noncovalent Interactions Assisted Catalysis in
Confinement
Supramolecular self-assembled capsules, cages, and cavitands
are unique architectures with a variety of shapes and rigid
frameworks to host diversified substrates of various sizes, in a
solvent-free microenvironment that provides utmost regulation
on the reaction outcomes through a combination of confine-
ment and noncovalent weak interactions.[43] Such entrapment
resembles substrates within the active site of enzymatic pockets
where high rates of selective conversions under mild conditions
are effected through a combined approach of optimum fitting
and secondary effects of the protein scaffolds.[44] Specifically,
confinement within restricted space in enzyme pockets prohibits
diffusional freedom of substrates, resulting in a greater propen-
sity to chemically react. Similarly, organic molecules adsorbed
in supramolecular pores and cavities have greater access to
each other, guided by dispersion forces. As a result, the trapped
molecules orient themselves in such a way that transition states
are stabilized compared to unconstrained possibilities, accelerat-
ing the overall rate of the reaction (Figure 11).[44] Nevertheless,
in some cases van der Waals interactions could be predominant,
and transition states could be stabilized or destabilized, or reac-
tants could have greater binding to the catalytic site, resulting
in a constraint-stabilized reactant state that decreases the reac-
tion rate (Figure 11). Sometimes, the transition state geometry is
difficult to accommodate in the available cavity volume and is
therefore destabilized due to entropic penalties.[45]

5. Summary and Outlook
In this article, we summarize the development of strategies to
exploit noncovalent weak interactions to control enantio-, regio-
, and chemo- selectivity in both molecular and supramolecular
organo-catalytic domains.[50] In most of the examples in this arti-
cle, it is found that the locally electrostatic H-bond together
with π dispersion interactions, combined with other favorable
forces such as the net attractive electrostatic X-bond, elucidates
the broad range of catalysis, and provides inspiration for sub-
tle modulation of different NCIs to amplify reactivity. In addition,
purely electrostatic effects, such as ion-pair interactions, have
also turned out to be remarkably powerful to achieve stereo-
induction. However, the stereoselectivity-determining transition
state is controlled by the cooperative effect of several nonco-
valent interactions, which makes it difficult to identify a dom-
inant one. Moreover, there is a fine line partitioning favorable
noncovalent interactions and unfavorable steric interactions,
which sometimes impose challenges on the stereoselective
transformations.
The basic understanding integrating attractive NCIs into
small molecule scaffolds and interpreting transition state struc-
tures aided by DFT studies provide valuable insights. Addi-
tionally, topological and structure-oriented parameters lead to
analysis of weak interactions. In general, the contribution of elec-
tronic structure theory in understanding the atomistic origin of
cooperative function has been phenomenal. For instance, during
intramolecular Michael cyclization of a prochiral cyclohexanone,
Paton’s truncated thiourea prefers a syn-coplanar conformation
(CNCH 31°) over an anti-periplanar conformation (CNCH 178°)
due to favorable H-bonds in the corresponding transition state
(O···HN = 1.95 Å in syn versus 2.03 Å in anti). This leads to
an intrinsic barrier drop of about 4 kcal/mol. Furthermore, in
cinchona alkaloid based α-quaternary stereo-induction and flu-
orination of an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde shows that H-bond
network with MeSO3−counter-anion results in stronger non-
classical C─HO contacts in the transition-state mode resulting
in R product (2.232 Å) than that in the S-product (2.422 Å).
Wiberg bond order indices further point out that C─HO is
stronger in 0.0141 TS-R than in TS-S (0.0099). Obviously, this
leads to ∼0.6 kcal/mol preference for the R-stereoisomer. In
addition, enantioselective control in photoredox catalysis shows
how NCIs modulate reactions involving radical intermediates. In
cinchona-catalyst promoted photochemical pefluoroalkylation, it
was revealed that the enantioselective transition state models
for CF3• electrophilic attack on β-ketoesters resides within an
open-pocket of the catalyst-cation, that ensures that the O–H···O
interaction along the prochiral si-face (1.69 Å) is shorter than
along the re-face (1.74 Å), leading to a stabilized reactant complex
in the former (−14.0 kcal/mol versus –12.1 kcal/mol). It is specu-
lated that this extent of H-bonding is responsible for a favorable
attack from the si face of the enolate, leading to the targeted
“S” conformer. Reactions within confinement are also found to
provide regioselective outcomes such as Michael reaction in a
pentameric resorcinarene capsule, that captures the symbiosis
between halogen bonding and confinement effect. While the
energetic requirement for the X-bonded Michael addition inside
the capsule turned out to be 20.2 kcal/mol, the absence of halo-
gen bonding increases it to 26.4 kcal/mol, while the absence of
the entrapment builds up an additional 2 kcal/mol, indicating
the pivotal role of both attractive van der Waals in confinement
coupled to halogen bonding necessary for the desired result.
Quantitative theoretical understanding of how NCIs mani-
fest in molecules and their influence on bulk properties helps
to model accurate methods to extrapolate their effects all
the way to macromolecular structures or supramolecular self-
assemblage, relevant to the fields of materials and biology. This
leads to rapid experimental advances in the design of opti-
mum, new age, “smart” catalysts where noncovalent interactions
are pivotal. However, the failure of a range of density function-
als to accurately model dispersion forces and the inadequacy
of exchange-correlation functionals to accurately handle sys-
tems consisting of >500 atoms make it cautionary on functional
choice for further studies. Moreover, in computations where
